358.title: A hundred years asleep
358.hook: a man passes a ruined town, dies a hundred years, and wakes to see his donkey raised (2:259)
358.carry: he can revive what is dead
358.howItsDone: Muslims read 2:258–260 together as three stories about God giving life to the dead, and often recall them when speaking of resurrection and of hope after loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no compulsion, and your line, a handhold you grasp yourself. Today, a man asks a hard question out loud, and is answered with a story he lives through.

A traveler rides his donkey past a town that's been destroyed: roofs fallen in, walls collapsed onto themselves, nobody left. He's carrying some food and something to drink. He stops, looks at the ruins, and says what anyone might say: how could God ever bring this back to life? The text doesn't say whether he asks it in wonder or in doubt. And then, the Qur'an says, he finds out. Today: a hundred years asleep.
screen: `A RUINED TOWN, NOBODY LEFT.` → `HOW COULD THIS EVER LIVE AGAIN?` → `THEN HE FINDS OUT.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred fifty-nine goes on: God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him, and asked: how long have you stayed? He answered: a day, or part of a day. That's how waking feels. No, a hundred years. Look at your food and drink: they haven't spoiled. Look at your donkey. And look at the bones, how We set them together and clothe them with flesh. When it became clear to him, he said: I know that God has power over all things. The Qur'an doesn't name the man or the town. The commentators offer names: some say 'Uzayr, whom some identify with Ezra, and the town Jerusalem after its destruction; others name the prophet Jeremiah, or someone else. The story works without a name. Look at the details it does give. The food is unchanged after a century. The donkey, in one reading, has gone to bones and comes back; other commentators read the bones as the man's own. One thing time didn't touch, one thing it took completely, and in the story both are in God's hands. And look where the story sits. Just before it, Ibrahim tells a king: my Lord gives life and causes death. Just after it, Ibrahim asks to see how the dead are raised, and is shown with four birds. Three stories in a row about the same question. The man's question isn't scolded. It's answered with a demonstration he lives through.
screen: `A DAY, OR PART OF A DAY` · `THE FOOD UNSPOILED, THE DONKEY RAISED` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T NAME HIM` · `THREE STORIES, ONE QUESTION`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something old coming back to life, a tree leafing after winter, a friendship starting again, a skill returning to your hands, and look closely at what was dead and what's stirring now. If you pray, hold it up with the man's last words: I know that God has power over all things.
'Uzayr. The name some commentators give the man who doubted a ruined town could live, was made to die a century, and woke to see his donkey raised. Today's word.
Your line: he can revive what is dead. A ruin isn't the end of the story. See you tomorrow.

359.title: Seven ears of grain
359.hook: a gift in Allah's way is like a grain that grows seven ears, a hundred grains each (2:261)
359.howItsDone: Muslims give sadaqah, voluntary charity, in amounts large and small, often citing 2:261 and the hadith that even a date given from honest earnings grows like a mountain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'Uzayr, a hundred years asleep, and your line, he can revive what is dead. Today, life again, out of a single seed.

Pull one stalk of wheat from a field and look at the top. The ear is packed with grains in neat rows. Any farmer knows the trade: one grain in the ground, and months later you hold dozens. Arithmetic and hope in the same handful. Right after three stories about God bringing the dead to life, al-Baqarah turns to the field and does some arithmetic of its own.
screen: `ONE STALK OF WHEAT.` → `ONE GRAIN IN, DOZENS OUT.` → `AL-BAQARAH DOES THE ARITHMETIC.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred sixty-one, in Pickthall's words: “The likeness of those who spend their wealth in Allah's way is as the likeness of a grain which groweth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains.” Do the math: seven hundred. And the verse adds: God multiplies for whom He wills. Seven hundred isn't the ceiling. The placement matters. The surah has just shown a dead town, a donkey's bones, four birds, all brought to life. Now a seed, buried and dead-looking, brings up a field. Giving is pictured the same way: let go into the ground, lost-looking, and coming back multiplied. Two hadith fill in the picture. A hadith qudsi in Bukhari and Muslim says a good deed is written as ten, up to seven hundred times, and many times more. Another, in Bukhari, says that whoever gives even the value of a single date from honest earnings, God accepts it with His right hand and raises it the way one of you raises a young horse, until it becomes like a mountain. One date. The grain in the verse is tiny too. Nothing here asks for a large gift. It asks for a real one, given for God's sake, from what's honestly yours, and then let go. In the verse, the arithmetic is God's.
screen: `ONE GRAIN, SEVEN EARS, A HUNDRED EACH` · `NOT THE CEILING` · `BURIED, LOST-LOOKING, MULTIPLIED` · `ONE DATE BECOMES A MOUNTAIN`

Your line: one grain, seven hundred. The gift can be as small as a date. I'll keep a seat for you.

360.title: Don't spoil it with reminders
360.hook: a kind word is better than charity followed by hurt (2:263–264)
360.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to give without reminding the recipient or expecting thanks; mann, recounting one's favors, is counted a serious fault, and many give quietly so as not to be tempted toward it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sunbulah, the ear of grain, and your line, one grain, seven hundred. Today, how a gift can be lost after it's given.

Remember when I drove the truck? Remember who paid for the pizza? A relative helped someone move years ago, and mentions it at every holiday since. The help was real: a whole Saturday, a borrowed truck, a sore back. But somewhere around the tenth reminder, the help starts to feel like a bill, a debt that can never be paid off. Al-Baqarah knows this relative.
screen: `REMEMBER WHEN I DROVE THE TRUCK?` → `MENTIONED AT EVERY HOLIDAY.` → `A GIFT TURNED INTO A DEBT.`

segments.voice: Right after the seven ears of grain, the surah adds a condition. Verse two hundred sixty-two: those who spend and don't follow it with reminders of their generosity, or with hurt, their reward is with their Lord. Verse two hundred sixty-three, in Pickthall's words: “A kind word with forgiveness is better than almsgiving followed by injury.” The Arabic for those reminders is mann: bringing up the favor, holding it over someone. Verse two sixty-four pictures what mann does. A smooth rock with a thin layer of soil on it. It looks like a field. Heavy rain falls and washes it bare. Nothing grows: there was only stone underneath. The next verse paints the opposite. A garden on high ground. Heavy rain falls, and it doubles its fruit; if no heavy rain comes, a light drizzle is enough. That's the gift given for God's sake, with no strings: it grows whatever the weather. The tradition takes mann seriously. A hadith in Sahih Muslim names three people God will not speak to on the Day of Judgment, and one is al-mannan, the one who reminds people of what he gave. And notice what the verse ranks above a spoiled gift: a kind word. Something gentle, with no money at all, is better than money with a sting.
screen: `NO REMINDERS, NO HURT` · `A KIND WORD IS BETTER` · `THE ROCK WASHED BARE` · `THE GARDEN ON THE HILL`

Mann. Reminding someone of a favor, holding it over them — what al-Baqarah says washes a gift away like rain off a bare rock. Today's word.
Your line: give and forget. A kind word can be the whole gift. Day three hundred sixty, done.

361.title: Write it down
361.hook: the longest verse is about recording debts fairly, with witnesses (2:282)
361.tomorrow: Not beyond what you can bear
361.howItsDone: Muslims draw on 2:282 for writing down loans and contracts with witnesses, and Islamic commercial law developed detailed rules for documentation from it; 2:280 adds the duty to give time to a debtor in hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mann, the reminders that spoil a gift, and your line, give and forget. Today, the opposite instruction, for a different kind of money.

Two old friends. One lends the other a few thousand dollars on a handshake, because writing it down would feel like distrust. A year later, one remembers a loan to be repaid by spring; the other remembers help, to be paid back someday. Neither is lying. The friendship doesn't survive the difference. What do you expect the longest verse in the Qur'an to be about? Heaven? The prophets? It's about this.
screen: `A LOAN ON A HANDSHAKE.` → `TWO HONEST MEMORIES.` → `THE LONGEST VERSE IS ABOUT THIS.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred eighty-two, in Pickthall's words: “O ye who believe! When ye contract a debt for a fixed term, record it in writing.” Then comes more detail than almost anywhere in the Qur'an. Let a scribe write it between you, in fairness, and not refuse. Let the one who owes dictate, so the record is in the borrower's own words, leaving nothing out. If the borrower is of weak understanding, or weak, or unable, a guardian dictates fairly. Bring witnesses. Don't be too weary to write it down, small or large, with its due date. The reason: this is more just with God, more upright as testimony, and more likely to keep you from doubt. Everyday trade, hand to hand on the spot, needn't be written. And no scribe or witness is to be harmed for doing the job. Yesterday: give and forget. Today: lend and write. They don't contradict. A gift should be forgotten by the giver; a debt should be remembered by both, exactly, so a fuzzy memory doesn't break a friendship or a faith. And just two verses earlier, al-Baqarah adds mercy: if the one who owes is in hardship, give them time, and if you let it go as charity, that's better for you. Write it down so it's fair; forgive it if they can't pay. Both sit a few lines apart in the same surah.
screen: `RECORD IT IN WRITING` · `THE BORROWER DICTATES` · `GIVE AND FORGET; LEND AND WRITE` · `IN HARDSHIP, GIVE THEM TIME`

segments.voice: Let the things you owe surface: a loan, yes, but also a favor to return, a promised visit, a book to give back, a reply someone's waiting for. Choose one and picture writing it clearly: what, to whom, by when. If you're the one owed, picture writing that down too, and decide whether, in someone's hardship, you'd give them time.
Kitab. Book, from the root k-t-b — the longest verse in the Qur'an, telling believers to put every debt in writing. Today's word.
Your line: lend and write. A clear record protects the friendship, and the faith. Until tomorrow.

362.title: Not beyond what you can bear
362.hook: Allah burdens no soul beyond its capacity, our Lord, forgive us (2:286)
362.carry: not beyond what I can bear
362.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last two verses of al-Baqarah (2:285–286) every night before sleeping, following a hadith that they suffice whoever reads them at night; the requests of 2:286 are also said often in personal supplication.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kitab, the long verse on debts, and your line, lend and write. Today, the last verse of al-Baqarah.

Al-Baqarah is two hundred eighty-six verses long. Laws, stories, warnings, arguments: the cow, Ayat al-Kursi, a man asleep for a hundred years, a debt written down. And at the very end it does something unexpected. It stops talking to people and turns into words people say back. Its last verse is a list of requests, and it opens with a promise about weight.
screen: `286 VERSES.` → `LAWS, STORIES, A DEBT.` → `THE END TURNS INTO A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, the verse opens: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The Arabic for scope is wus'a, capacity, the room a thing has inside it. Every soul has a size, and what's asked of it fits inside. Then the requests, each starting with our Lord. Don't take us to task if we forget or slip. Don't lay on us a burden like the one laid on those before us. Don't make us carry what we have no strength for. Pardon us, forgive us, have mercy on us. There's a story behind it, in Sahih Muslim. When the verse before, 2:284, came down, saying God will call people to account for what's in their hearts, shown or hidden, the companions were frightened. They came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ on their knees and said this was more than they could carry. He told them to say instead: we hear and we obey. They said it, and then these last two verses came. A related report in the same collection, from Ibn Abbas, says that after each request, God answered: I have done so. A hadith in Bukhari adds that whoever recites these last two verses at night, they will be enough for him; scholars read enough as protection, as a night prayer, or both. So the surah ends where some people end their day, in bed, saying these two verses. It doesn't promise that nothing will be heavy. It says the weight was measured to the one carrying it.
screen: `NOT BEYOND ITS SCOPE: WUS'A, CAPACITY` · `OUR LORD: A LIST OF REQUESTS` · `THE FRIGHTENED COMPANIONS` · `ENOUGH FOR THE NIGHT` · then, large: `ALLAH TASKETH NOT A SOUL BEYOND ITS SCOPE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that feels heavy right now; don't solve it, just notice how big it is, and that you're still here, holding it. On each out-breath, let the line be there: not beyond what I can bear. If you pray, you can add the verse's own words: our Lord, pardon us.
Wus'a. Capacity, the room a soul has inside it — al-Baqarah's closing promise that nothing asked exceeds it. Today's word.
Your line: not beyond what I can bear. In the report, the frightened companions were answered: I have done so. That's al-Baqarah, start to finish.

363.title: Clear and ambiguous
363.hook: some verses are clear, the foundation, others open to many meanings (3:7)
363.carry: some verses are for sitting with
363.howItsDone: Muslim scholars read the Qur'an's clear (muhkam) verses as its foundation and interpret the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses in their light; many ordinary believers simply affirm that all of it is from God and leave hard verses to further study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: wus'a, capacity, in the last verse of al-Baqarah, and your line, not beyond what I can bear. Today, a new surah.

A hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the first two long surahs a shared nickname: the two bright ones. Al-Baqarah, just finished, and Al 'Imran, the Family of Imran, starting today. Almost at once, before telling a single story, it stops to talk about reading itself. Not every verse in this book works the same way. Some are meant to be clear. Some are meant to be lived with.
screen: `THE TWO BRIGHT ONES.` → `AL 'IMRAN: THE FAMILY OF IMRAN.` → `A VERSE ABOUT READING.`

segments.voice: Here's 3:7 in Pickthall's words. God has revealed the Scripture "wherein are clear revelations - they are the substance of the Book - and others (which are) allegorical." The clear verses are muhkamat, from muhkam: made firm, tightly built. The root h-k-m also gives hikma, wisdom, and hakim, a judge. The verse calls them umm al-kitab, literally the mother of the Book: the foundation everything else rests on. The others are mutashabihat, verses that resemble one another and can be read more than one way. Then two kinds of readers. Those with a swerve in their hearts chase the ambiguous verses, looking for trouble and hunting a hidden meaning. Those firmly rooted in knowledge say: we believe in it; all of it is from our Lord. The commentators have long discussed one detail. The verse says no one knows its interpretation except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge. Where do you pause? Stop after God, and only God knows the meaning; the learned simply trust. Read straight on, and the learned know something of it too. Respected scholars have held both, and both pauses are known in recitation. Which verses count as ambiguous is discussed too: some name the letters that open certain surahs, some name verses about God's attributes, or the unseen. So the verse doesn't ask you to understand everything. It gives you a floor to stand on, and permission to leave some verses open without forcing them.
screen: `MUHKAM: MADE FIRM` · `THE MOTHER OF THE BOOK` · `TWO KINDS OF READERS` · `WHERE DO YOU PAUSE?` · then, large: `ALL OF IT IS FROM OUR LORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a line, from any book, that you don't understand or that troubles you a little, and hold it loosely, the way you'd hold something fragile that isn't yours, without arguing with it. Then think of one line that's firm for you and let it be the ground you sit on: firm ground underneath, an open question in your hands.
Muhkam. Made firm, clear, tightly built. The muhkamat are the clear verses, the mother of the Book, from 3:7. Today's word.
Your line: some verses are for sitting with. Not every question needs an answer today. Al 'Imran has begun.

364.title: Don't let our hearts swerve
364.hook: our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You guided us (3:8)
364.howItsDone: Many Muslims say the supplication of 3:8, 'rabbana la tuzigh qulubana', after the daily prayers and in personal du'a, along with the Prophet's reported prayer to the Turner of hearts.

segments.voice: Yesterday: muhkam, the firm verses, the mother of the Book, and your line, some verses are for sitting with.

Yesterday's verse carried a warning: some have a swerve in their hearts, and chase what's unclear. The very next verse doesn't point a finger at them. It turns around and asks for help. Commentators hear the people just praised, those firmly rooted in knowledge, as the ones speaking. Their first worry isn't other people's hearts. It's their own. If anyone could feel safe from drifting, it's them. They don't.
screen: `A SWERVE IN THE HEART.` → `THE NEXT VERSE TURNS AROUND.` → `NOT THEIR HEARTS. OURS.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's translation, 3:8 begins: "Our Lord! Cause not our hearts to stray after Thou hast guided us." Then it asks for mercy from God's own presence, and ends: You are the Bestower. Notice the link. Yesterday's verse said zaygh, a swerve, in the hearts of some. Today's asks la tuzigh, don't let them swerve. Same root, z-y-gh: to lean, to tilt away from straight. One verse describes the tilt; the next asks to be kept from it. Notice the timing too: after You guided us. It's a prayer for people who've already found the way and know that finding it once isn't the same as staying on it. A hadith in Tirmidhi reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ often said: O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon your religion. Anas, who reports it, says the companions asked whether he feared for them, and he said yes: hearts are held between two of God's fingers, and He turns them as He wills. Turner of hearts is muqallib al-qulub, and both words share one root, q-l-b, to turn over: the heart is named as the thing that turns. Some Muslims say 3:8 in their supplications after the prayer. And it closes a week about keeping things: a man raised after a hundred years, a grain that multiplies, a gift unspoiled, a debt written down, a burden that fits, verses held firm or held open. Today, a heart kept straight.
screen: `THE SWERVE, AND THE REQUEST` · `Z-Y-GH: TO TILT AWAY` · `AFTER YOU GUIDED US` · `QALB: THE THING THAT TURNS` · then, large: `OUR LORD! CAUSE NOT OUR HEARTS TO STRAY.`

segments.voice: Sit up straight and feel how small the movements are that keep you upright, a lean forward, a correction back; nobody sits perfectly still. Think of one place this week where your heart tilted a little, toward impatience, envy or carelessness, and without scolding it, notice the lean and come back to center. If you pray, you can say 3:8 in Arabic or your own language: rabbana la tuzigh qulubana.
Zaygh, a swerve in the heart. The request of 3:8, la tuzigh, asks not to let it happen, made by people already guided, who want to stay that way. Today's word.
Your line: keep my heart straight. A lean you notice is a lean you can correct. That's a week, done.
